33.23.4.en: Since the Lord took weakness upon Himself and bore our punishment by His death, He restored our corruption by His resurrection.

33.23.6.en: "Deliver him" is the literal translation of the Hebrew word "redeem him," that is, to rescue a person by a ransom or by paying a price on his behalf. The Greek word means paying a price or a ransom, and it is used in (Mt 20:28): "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."

33.23.7.en: The speech here is a clear prophecy of the eternal redemption whose price the Lord Christ paid with His precious blood. As the Apostle Paul says: "Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us" (Heb 9:12).

33.23.8.en: "I have found a ransom": our Lord Jesus has found this redemption. The expression "found" points to His burning zeal for the salvation of the world, His faithfulness, His joy, and His striving for the salvation of man. He works like one who searches until he finds, and then rejoices!

33.23.9.en: "Go after that which is lost, until he find it. And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing" (Lk 15:4-5).

33.23.10.en: "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost" (Lk 15:6).

33.23.11.en: "What woman... if she lose one piece... seek diligently till she find it" (Lk 15:8).

33.23.12.en: [Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost] (Lk 15:9).

33.23.13.en: "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him" (Ps 89:20).

33.23.14.en: * The Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, shows mercy to man, having taken the form of a man. Through His tenderness He says to His Father on behalf of the man who is saved: [Deliver him from going down to corruption]...

33.24.s.en: 4. The sweetness of enjoying God's salvation

33.24.0.en: 25 His flesh shall be fresher than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth. 26 He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness. 27 He shall sing among men, and say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not. 28 He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light. 29 "Lo, all these things worketh God oftentimes with man, 30 To bring back his soul from the pit, to be enlightened with the light of the living.

33.24.1.en: His flesh shall be fresher (more flourishing) than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth [25].

33.24.2.en: When Elihu spoke of Christ the Redeemer, he lifted our eyes from tribulations, sorrows, and sicknesses to what we enjoy through this wonderful redemption. Instead of speaking about sicknesses, Elihu marvels as he sees, in the spirit of prophecy, the man who was descending toward eternal destruction not only enjoying health, but his body becoming fresher than the body of a child, changed from the state of helpless old age to strong youth, full of vitality and energy.

33.24.3.en: Through redemption he enjoys a new birth, and the believer becomes a new creation after the image of his Creator. He becomes a son of God in the waters of Baptism, by his union with the Only-Begotten Son. He becomes a new Naaman, of whom it was said: "Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean" (2 Kgs 5:14). The saying of the Lord Christ to Nicodemus is fulfilled in him: "Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" (Jn 3:5-6).

33.24.4.en: * [His flesh was consumed by punishments, that it may return to the days of his youth] [25]. When the first man fell from the presence of God, we were driven out from the delights of Paradise and bound to the miseries of this perishable life. And we feel the pain of our punishment, how grave is the fault we committed through the serpent's deception. For having fallen into this state, we find nothing outside God but sorrow... We suffer daily sorrow in the flesh, with its torment and death. Therefore the Lord, by His wonderful dispensation, changes what befell us through our commission of sin, by means of punishment....

33.24.5.en: [His flesh was consumed by punishments, that it may return to the days of his youth]. It is as though he said: Through the punishment of death (the death of man) he has sunk down in his old age; let him return to the days of his youth, that is, let him be renewed to the fullness of his former life, and not remain in the state into which he fell, but by his salvation return to the delights of the state in which he was originally created... Since we were brought to this power of new life not by our own strength but by the Savior, may the Messenger (the Lord Christ) say in His mediation for this man who is under punishment: [Let him return to the days of his youth].

33.25.0.en: He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness [26].

33.25.1.en: By this new birth the believer enters into a relationship with God, as a son who has boldness before his father. He prays, confesses, praises, and gives thanks, offering sweet incense that God smells as a fragrance of delight and acceptance, by virtue of the sacrifice of Christ. He looks to God his Father with joy of heart, seeing His face with shouting and rejoicing. He does not fear meeting Him, for he knows the truth of the reconciliation accomplished by the Cross.

33.25.2.en: God pours out on His believers the fruits of the Spirit in abundance, so that they bear the icon of Christ and His righteousness.

33.25.3.en: Thus Elihu moves us from crying out because of sorrows to shouting as sons of the heavenly Father, bearing the new nature crowned with glory, enjoying the sight of God's face, sharing with the heavenly beings in their praises and shouts, and being covered by the righteousness of Christ, which we put on as a radiant heavenly garment.

33.25.4.en: * [He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him]. He says that the Messenger (the propitiating Intercessor) intercedes first and then man. For if the Lord had not interceded with His Father through His incarnation and prayed for our life, our living stiffness could not have been moved to seek the eternal things... But because the light of truth bursts forth with hidden joy in our hearts after trials, often after great sorrows, it is rightly added concerning this man who has been tried and who pleads with God: "And he shall see his face with joy" [25]. It was said earlier how God works by revealing Himself to us; here it shows how He delights us when He makes Himself known.

33.25.5.en: Thus Jacob, after his struggle with the angel, said: "I have seen God face to face" (Gen 32:30), as one who says: {I know the Lord because He Himself condescends to make me know Him}. But Paul declares that this knowledge will be accomplished in its utmost perfection at the end, where he says: "then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:12). After the struggle in toils and the waves of trials, the soul is often carried away rejoicing as it contemplates the knowledge of the divine presence (which it can sense but cannot enjoy in its fullness). Therefore it is rightly said of this man who has been tried after many toils: "He shall see his face with joy" [26]. The more a man contemplates divine things, the more he is repaid for his earthly deeds by the grace of contemplation; therefore it is fitting that it be added for his works: "for he will render unto man his righteousness" [26].

33.25.6.en: It is called "our righteousness" not as though it were from ourselves, but because it has become ours by divine gift, as we say in the Lord's Prayer: [Give us this day our daily bread](b). Behold, we call it "our bread" although we pray that we may receive it. It becomes ours when we receive it, but it belongs to God, because it is He who gives it.

33.25.8.en: He shall sing among men, and say:

33.26.0.en: I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not [27].

33.26.1.en: The phrase in the Hebrew is "he sings among men," and the translations of the Hebrew word Shiyr שִׁיר, meaning "to sing," differ. Man is transformed from his crying out under the intensity of the trials and sufferings that befell him into rejoicing and praising, singing of the grace of this Mediator who redeemed him, renewed his nature by His Holy Spirit, and granted him eternal life. He sinned and perverted the straight way, but grace covered him, so he received forgiveness and was not repaid for his past.

33.26.2.en: Some have seen that the Hebrew word is derived from שׁוּר Shuwr, meaning "to look around" or "to regard" or "to observe." Therefore the English translation (KJ*) came: [He looketh upon men, and if any say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not]. This phrase seems to point to the divine Mediator, the Savior of the world, who looks upon corrupted humanity; if anyone confesses that he has sinned and has spoiled what is good of the abilities and possibilities, and of the mercies and blessings given to him by the Savior, and that this has not profited him at all, the Savior will work in him.

33.26.3.en: Whether under the pressure of trials or in the enjoyment of seeing the Mediator, if anyone confesses the sins and crookedness of his conduct, he enjoys the divine mercies.

33.26.4.en: In this Elihu presents to us his view of trials as discipline from the Lord, whose aim is that man may return to himself, discover his faults, and feel his need of the Redeemer, and so enjoy the divine mercies.

33.26.5.en: By saying "perverted that which was right," he may mean: I misjudged God's plan toward me. Trials are permitted me for the uprightness of my life, but because of the corruption of my heart I looked upon them as an injustice that had befallen me. For this reason "it profited me not" or "I was not repaid for it." The fault is not in the coming of trials but in my not profiting from them because of my murmuring against the Lord, and I reckoned that I did not deserve all these harsh sufferings.

33.26.6.en: * [He looketh upon men, and saith, I have sinned] [27]. He could not have known that he was a sinner if righteousness had not come to him. For no one discovers his faults unless he has begun to be upright. One who is wholly deformed cannot perceive the truth about himself. But the one who feels that he is a sinner has already, to some degree, begun to become upright. Being upright, he blames his conduct where he is still not righteous. And by accusing himself he begins to cleave to God. And as he passes on to accusing himself in truth, he condemns himself in what he perceives does not please God.

33.26.7.en: But if a sinner looks at himself without having learned the character of the righteous man, he cannot by any means perceive that he is a sinner...

33.26.9.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the believer, as he looks upon men (the saints), reads in their lives as in an open book, and so perceives that he is a sinner and offers repentance so that he may live in the righteousness of Christ. In his comment on this phrase he says: [The lives of the righteous are a living study; therefore it is not without merit that the righteous are called "books" in the language of Scripture, as it is written: "And the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works"

33.26.10.en: (Rev 2:12)... To acquire the knowledge of heavenly things we study the examples of the saints who went before us. It is said that they feed among the lilies (see Song 4:5-6). For what is meant by the lilies but the conduct of those who say in all sincerity: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ" (2 Cor 2:15)... For as long as we pass through the shadows of this perishable life until we reach the dawn of the eternal day, we need to be nourished by the examples of the righteous.]

33.26.11.en: * [He looketh upon men, and saith, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not, as I deserved] [27]. Even those who do not believe that they sin confess in a general way that they are sinners. So it is with men. They often confess openly that they are sinners, but when they hear someone truthfully mention their sins when they attack them, they boldly defend themselves and seek to show themselves innocent. Whoever has this character, when he says that he sins, does not speak the truth; he declares himself a sinner, but not from the depth of his heart, only uttering words, because it is written: [The righteous man is first in his own cause] (see Prov 18:17). He wishes to gain a good reputation, not to be humbled by confessing his sin. By accusing himself he desires to appear humble while he is not so... But the righteous man, when he accuses himself for his conduct, knows the depth of his heart, through the examples of the saints, that he is truly as he confesses. And in pain he completes: that he was not repaid as he deserved.

33.27.0.en: He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light [28].

33.27.1.en: This is the song of those who come out of the great tribulation (Rev 7:14), as they praise God for His surpassing mercies, who lifted them from the pit of hell to the heavenly Jerusalem, and brought them across from the kingdom of darkness to dwell in His bosom forever in the divine light. As it was said of the heavenly Jerusalem: [And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof] (Rev 21:23).

33.27.2.en: * [He will deliver his soul from going into destruction] [28]. When divine grace goes before us in good works, our free will follows it, and when we submit our consent to God who saves us, it is said of us that we redeem our own souls. Paul says: "I laboured more abundantly than they all" (1 Cor 15:10). And fearing that he might ascribe his labors to himself, he immediately added: "yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me." For since by his free will he followed the grace of God that went before him and protected him, he truly added: "which was with me," so that he might not be ungrateful for the divine grace, nor remain estranged from being made fit for free will...

33.27.3.en: "And his life shall see the light" [28], meaning the light of truth which he could not see when he was dead in his heart, or it means the Lord who said: "I am the light of the world" (Jn 8:12)...

33.28.0.en: Lo, all these things worketh God oftentimes with man [29].

33.28.1.en: Some translate "twice and thrice" as "many times," meaning that God does not cease to work for salvation once, twice, and thrice, and by every means, in order to draw the wicked to salvation, that they may enjoy sonship to Him and revel in His righteousness, His holiness, and His heavens.

33.28.2.en: Some see that Elihu mentions "thrice" as an indication of God's work with sinners, in which He uses three ways:

33.28.3.en: First He pours out good things in abundance, that man may be touched by the love of the Giver; if he does not return to God, He uses divine inspirations, whether through dreams, visions, or divine revelation; if he does not return, He uses sorrows and tribulations so that he may reconsider his life and realize the truth of his position.

33.28.4.en: * [Lo, all these things worketh God thrice with every man] [29]... If we observe carefully, we shall find that there are three stages of sorrow and joy, one following the other, in his conversion, in his trial, and in his death.

33.28.5.en: In the first occasion, his conversion... man's sorrow is great, because he takes his sins into account, and desires to cast off forcefully the bonds of worldly cares and to walk in the way of God throughout the period of his conversion. He wishes to remove the weight of heavy temporal disturbances in order to bear the easy yoke of the Lord. It is a bondage that bears freedom... But then comes pain of heart and its turmoil, as the Spirit calls from one side and the flesh calls him from the opposite side... Rightly it is said of this embittered man: "So that his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat. His soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers" [see 2, 22]. But divine grace does not allow us to be exposed to these hardships for a long time. It looses the bonds of our sins and leads us quickly to the consolations of the freedom of our new life. The joy that follows removes the former sorrow. And so the mind of the one who is converted rejoices very much more than it desires...

33.28.6.en: And lest man think that he is a saint, immediately upon his conversion... he is permitted by God's dispensation to suffer the assaults of trials. By his conversion he crosses the Red Sea, but the enemies continue to oppose him in the wilderness of this present life. We have left our past sins behind us, as the Egyptians died on the shore, but destructive vices still attack us like new enemies to obstruct our way by which we enter the Promised Land... Our enemy is more zealous against our victory as long as we are in this life, the more he perceives that we are rebelling against him. He does not care that he strikes those whom he knows to be in his possession. Rather, he is in a state of greater fury against us, since he has been driven out of our hearts, as though it were his right to possess us as a dwelling for himself... Truly there are three stages for the converted: the beginning, the middle, and the end. In the beginning they experience the charm of sweetness, in the middle the resistance of trials, and at the end the fullness of perfection...

33.28.7.en: After passing through these two stages, conversion and testing, in sorrow and joy, the third stage remains, whose sorrows he still fears, but whose delights he receives... David says: [And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified] (Ps 143:2). And Paul says after that: "For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified" (1 Cor 4:4). James says: "In many things we offend all" (Jas 3:2), and John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8)

33.29.0.en: To bring back his soul from the pit, to be enlightened with the light of the living [30].

33.29.1.en: Elihu here confirms what he had pointed out earlier as a song that man sings in enjoying God's salvation (Job 33:28): that it is a gift offered to every man without partiality, for God is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2 Pet 3:9). So every believer sings: "For thou hast delivered my soul from death: wilt not thou deliver my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of the living?" (Ps 56:13).

33.29.2.en: * Because the mind of every elect person suffers in each of these three stages, that is, the pain of conversion, the trials of testing, or the horror of dissolution, and is purified and set free by that very pain, it was said: [To bring back his soul from corruption, to be enlightened with the light of the living] [30].

33.29.3.en: For this is the light of the dead, which we behold with our bodily eyes... But those who are enlightened by the light of the living despise the light of the world and return to the height of the inner splendor, so that they may live in that place where they see and feel the true light, where there is no difference between life and light, for where there is light there is life also...

33.30.s.en: 5. An appeal to Job to listen to him

33.30.0.en: 31 Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak. 32 If thou hast any thing to say, answer me: speak, for I desire to justify thee. 33 If not, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom."

33.30.1.en: Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me:

33.30.2.en: hold thy peace, and I will speak [31].

33.30.3.en: Elihu asks Job to examine deeply what he has said and to listen with very close attention to what he is about to say. He has much to say, a matter that touches Job's life, which deserves that he be longsuffering and patient in earnest, to listen to what Elihu will say to him.

33.30.4.en: If thou hast any thing to say, answer me.

33.31.0.en: Speak, for I desire to justify thee [32].

33.31.1.en: Before Elihu continues his speech, which comes in the next chapter, he wanted to pause thoughtfully, asking Job to answer him or to offer his comments on what he has said.

33.31.2.en: Here Elihu's calmness stands out. Although he exaggerated in accusing Job, he stops to hear his comments in a good spirit. For his aim is neither to rebuke nor to heap accusations, but to open the door of salvation and righteousness so that Job may be justified before God. So it is fitting for us in our preaching to realize the truth of our message: not criticism and rebuke, but support and tenderness together with frankness and without flattery. Elihu had already said to Job that he too was formed out of the same clay, and that both of them need the Savior who helps. And the Apostle Peter says in his preaching to the first Gentile: "I myself also am a man" (Acts 10:26).

33.31.3.en: A man does not need someone to terrify him, but someone who is tender and gentle with him, and who makes him feel that he is a companion with him in human weakness, and needs with him the divine help.

33.31.4.en: In humility, love, and tenderness Elihu asks Job, if he has any objection or asks for clarification, to speak freely, for he wishes to explain in love all that is in his mind for the sake of Job's justification.

33.31.5.en: Just as Elihu asked Job to listen with longsuffering and patience to what Elihu has said and will say, he also declares his own readiness to listen with an open heart and longsuffering.

33.31.6.en: By saying "I desire to justify thee," Elihu feared that he might have misunderstood Job's statements, or attributed to him words with meanings that Job did not intend; therefore he gives him the opportunity to speak frankly.

33.32.0.en: Hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom [33].

33.32.1.en: If Job has nothing with which to object to Elihu's words, the latter demands that he listen to him and pay attention, and he will teach him wisdom.

33.32.2.en: Since Job kept silent, and none of the three friends intervened, Elihu wanted to continue his speech (as it comes in the next chapter).

33.32.3.en: Let my soul sing aloud to You,
